To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) phage challenge of L. monocytogene s selects for surviving clones with mutations in WTA glycosylation genes, (ii) loss of galactosyl residues from WTA and LTA leads to loss of InlB, (iii) InlB specifically binds to galactosides, and (iv) loss of Inl B leads to a loss of cellular invasiveness and virulence in vivo.

the serovar 1/4b specific antigen is a galactosyl-β-1,3-N-acetylglucosamine polymer that is crucial for phage adsorption to Listeria monocyto- genes and that this antigen is also crucial for Listeria monocyo- genes to interact with host cell receptors, and to be taken up by host cells.

Listeria monocytenes serovar (sv.) 4b strains are resistant to phage infection by virtue of their galactose-modified teichoic acids, and that these same molecules are required for InlB-dependent host cell invasion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the O-antigen in the interaction of Listeria with its natural host and with the bacteriophage.
the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underlie the ability of bacteria to invade and replicate inside host cells.
the mechanisms of host cell invasion, and the factors that contribute to bacterial pathogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
serovar 1/2a, 1/2b and 4b strains of Listeria monocygenes are able to attach and enter host cells by the InlA/InlB-mediated mechanism and are sensitive to phage 936.
the loss of a single galactose residue from the L. monocytogene 4b-specific teichoic acid polymer has a dramatic impact on both bacterial virulence and resistance to bacteriophage.
the L. monocytogenses 4b serovar is a unique serovar that is characterized by the presence of galactose residues in its WTA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Listeria monocygenes is a pathogen which is able to adapt to different environments.
L. monocytogene serovar 1/2a and 1/2b are sensitive to the bacteriophages P100, A500, and A511.
the Listeria monocitogenes serovars 4b and 4d differ only by their WTA glycosylation patterns, and that this subtle modification is crucial for the interaction with both phage and host cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the surface decoration of a pathogen is not just a passive shield against phage attack, but can also actively promote virulence.
the glycosylation pattern of Listeria monocygenes serovar-specific WTAs is essential for both phage resistance and pathogenicity.
L. monocytogens serovar 1/2a strains are more resistant to phages due to their ability to produce a WTA that is resistant to phage adsorption.
